summary_paragraph: A 68-year-old male with a history of multiple strokes, tracheostomy, GJ tube, atrial fibrillation, and recent UTI was admitted for fever and blood from his G-tube, initially brought in for routine replacement. Imaging showed no abdominal leak, but chest findings revealed bilateral lower lobe infiltrates concerning for hospital-associated pneumonia. He was treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics, and a mini-BAL identified Serratia marcescens and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Antibiotics were narrowed to levofloxacin, which he continued via G-tube. The G-tube was successfully replaced without complications. His white count improved, fever resolved, and he remained stable. C. diff was ruled out despite history. His atrial fibrillation was managed with warfarin, temporarily supported with heparin until therapeutic INR was achieved. A stage 2 sacral pressure ulcer was monitored with wound care. He was discharged to extended care on oral levofloxacin for a full 14-day course and with warfarin dose increased to 4mg daily, to be titrated by rehab based on INR.
